extracted.intended_audience: poets and writers composing epigrams/epitaphs and anyone interested in principles of literary praise
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short, pointed epigrams/epitaphs and for giving literary praise — what makes praise effective, honest, and artful in brief poetic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs as short pointed praise
rubrics_metrics.description: "a sort of Writing which is wholly set apart for a short pointed Method of Praise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epitaphs should be concise and pointed; their form is specifically to deliver praise in a brief, sharp manner. Use economy of words to make a single, memorable turn or observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground praise in real merit; avoid loose qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: "when they would praise, they cautiously avoid every looser Qualification, and fix only where there is a real Foundation in Merit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lavish vague or flattering phrases without basis. Anti-pattern: attributing qualities that are not supported by the subject's known deeds or character. Praise should be defensible and tied to observable merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid praise that depends on fable or false qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our Praise is trifling when it depends upon Fable; it is false when it depends upon wrong Qualifications; it means nothing when it is general."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on myth, legend, or mistaken facts as the basis of praise — such praise will not endure. Ensure factual/contextual accuracy; otherwise praise may be dismissed as hollow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be general; circumscribe praise to particular qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: "It would be better, if when we light upon such a Turn, we join it with something that circumscribes and bounds it to the Qualities of our Subject."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, bounded praise (naming characteristic deeds, styles, or local connections) is more convincing and valuable than broad, generic laudation. Example anti-pattern: a line that could apply to 'any great man' because it lacks particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone and humour of praise to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary on Anacreon: the writer 'has filled his own Head with the Character of his Subject... the Humour is easy and gay, resembling Anacreon in its Air.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When praising a particular author or subject, adopt a tone, register, or imagery sympathetic to that subject's character or oeuvre; this creates harmony between praise and praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of contemporary beliefs and audience reception
rubrics_metrics.description: On Orpheus: if one 'take the Fable for granted... the Turn appears to have Piety', but 'with respect to our present Knowledge, it will be less esteem'd.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conceit or turn that relies on beliefs no longer widely held may fall flat. Consider how current readers will interpret the image or premise; update references to avoid alienating or confusing the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony or satirical-appearance as an effective mode of praise
rubrics_metrics.description: "An Irony is look'd upon as the finest Palliative of Praise; and very often conveys the noblest Panegyrick under the Appearance of Satire."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect praise via irony or mock-accusation can be powerful: framing compliment as a mock rebuke or faux-critique can emphasize excellence while appearing modest or witty. Example: the epigram that treats Homer as a 'plagiary' which actually extols him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie praise to place, nation, or civic associations when apt
rubrics_metrics.description: On Menander: the epigram 'has also told the Country he was born in... while it twists together the Glory of the Poet and his Nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connecting an artist's qualities to their birthplace or nation can amplify praise by giving it communal or civic significance. Use this only when the connection is relevant and true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ surprising turns or raised scope judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Example on Homer: the poet 'slides by, and raises the whole World for a kind of Arbiter' — a move that enlarges scale unexpectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sudden enlargement of scope or an unexpected rhetorical pivot can elevate a short piece. Use such turns to astonish or reframe, but ensure they remain controlled and linked to the subject so as not to seem evasive or grandiose without basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the praise reflect intimate knowledge of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: On Anacreon and others: the writer 'has filled his own Head with the Character of his Subject' and the epigram 'has a respect to the Character of its Subject... Menander writ remarkably with a Justness and Purity of Language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective praise demonstrates familiarity with the style, temper, and strengths of the praised person; imitating or echoing those qualities in the praise can be flattering and convincing. Anti-pattern: praise that shows the writer is a stranger to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear, proper English; avoid cant, jargon, and affected foreignisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Philonicus's complaint: 'they should let their Clients have a little decent and proper English... correct such an illiberal Cant among profess'd Speakers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain, proper language appropriate to the audience rather than obscure legalese, cant, or gratuitous foreign phrases. Clarity preserves dignity and makes praise accessible to its intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epitaphs (and self-addressed verses) to teach graceful retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowley's epitaph 'is an Instruction how to leave the Publick with a good Grace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epitaph can serve not only to praise but to model a modest, philosophic attitude toward mortality and public life. When composing such pieces, balance wit and humility to provide moral or instructive closure.
